subject: physics

moments.title: Carnot's reflections
moments.body:
Sadi Carnot, 28 years old, publishes 'Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu'. He asks the question: what is the maximum efficiency of a heat engine?

He answers: an idealised cyclic engine operating between two temperatures (hot Th, cold Tc) has efficiency at most 1 - Tc/Th, regardless of the working substance. Any real engine does worse. The result holds even though Carnot is still working in the framework of the caloric theory (heat as a conserved fluid).
moments.takeaway: Even without correct theoretical foundations, Carnot deduces the central principle of heat engines.

moments.title: Carnot dies in obscurity
moments.body:
Carnot dies of cholera in the 1832 Paris epidemic at age 36. His personal effects, including notebooks, are burned for fear of contagion. His 1824 book had only sold 600 copies and was largely forgotten.

Clapeyron (1834) rediscovers and develops Carnot's ideas, putting them into mathematical form. They are taken up by Kelvin and Clausius in the 1840s and 1850s.
moments.takeaway: Almost the entire output of a foundational thinker is destroyed by a panicked health response.

moments.title: Clausius defines entropy
moments.body:
Clausius formalises Carnot's principle in terms of a new state function. He defines: change in entropy equals heat transferred divided by absolute temperature, dS = dQ/T (for reversible processes).

The second law of thermodynamics: entropy of an isolated system never decreases. In 1865 he gives entropy its name (from the Greek for 'transformation').

quote.text: Die Energie der Welt ist konstant; die Entropie der Welt strebt einem Maximum zu. (The energy of the world is constant; the entropy of the world tends toward a maximum.)

moments.takeaway: Energy is conserved (first law); usable energy is not (second law). The arrow of time has a name.

moments.title: Boltzmann's statistical interpretation
moments.body:
Boltzmann shows that entropy is a measure of the number of microscopic configurations consistent with a given macroscopic state. S = k log W. Entropy increase is statistical inevitability — disordered configurations are vastly more numerous than ordered ones.

Boltzmann's interpretation reduces a phenomenological law to a counting argument. It also opens the door to statistical mechanics. The formula S = k log W is engraved on his grave.
moments.takeaway: Macroscopic thermodynamic laws emerge from microscopic statistics. Reductionism wins another round.

moments.title: Boltzmann's suicide
moments.body:
Boltzmann's atomistic and statistical interpretation of physics was bitterly opposed by Mach, Ostwald and the 'energeticists' who rejected atoms as unobservable speculation. Boltzmann suffered chronic depression.

On holiday in Duino in 1906, Boltzmann hanged himself. His wife and daughter found him. Within a few years atomism was definitively confirmed by Einstein's analysis of Brownian motion (1905) and Perrin's experiments. He didn't live to see it.
moments.takeaway: Boltzmann died before his interpretation was vindicated. He never knew he was right.

now.title: Thermodynamics today
now.body:
Thermodynamics is the most foundational physical theory we have — it survives every paradigm shift. Even quantum field theory and general relativity must satisfy thermodynamic laws.

Applications span every branch of science: refrigeration, internal combustion engines, biological metabolism, information theory (Shannon entropy is mathematically identical to Boltzmann's), black hole thermodynamics (Bekenstein, Hawking), the early universe.
now.open_questions: Why does the universe seem to have started in a low-entropy state? (We don't know.) Can we make engines that approach Carnot efficiency in practice? How does entropy relate to information in quantum systems? Is the third law (S → 0 as T → 0) really fundamental, or an artefact of how we define entropy?

reflection: Carnot died at 36 with his work unrecognised. Boltzmann killed himself a year before the atomistic worldview he championed was confirmed. Both founded thermodynamics; both lived in the shadow of resistance from their contemporaries. What does it say about science that its foundations were laid by people who didn't see their work accepted in their lifetimes?
